Let's obviously we're in an election year, you do run unopposed. What do you see is the biggest issue locally? You represent a district with very wide range of economics and the social different neighborhoods. What do you see locally is the biggest issue in Massachusetts?

Two things. First, the cost of living. It is too expensive to heat your home, to fill up your gas tank, to get groceries, to pay for medicines, costs for almost everything across the economy have gone up. In Massachusetts, in particular, housing is really driving inflation. Massachusetts has an affordable housing crisis. Since my time as a city councilor and Newton on the land use committee now up to my service as vice chair of the financial services committee which has jurisdiction over housing. I have constantly been advocating for liberalizing our zoning rules so we can build more multi-family housing in Massachusetts. And also for putting more resources behind public-private partnerships to make more housing permanently affordable. Massachusetts needs to build hundreds of thousands of new units of housing until, and unless we do that, housing costs are going to continue to price people out of living in the base state, make it too hard for young people to get started at home, make it too hard for older Americans to downsize into the kinds of amenity-rich apartments that they're looking for, we need to build more housing in this state. Number two is largely due to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. We've seen energy prices skyrocket throughout the United States, but particularly in Massachusetts for more than any other state in the union is highly sensitive to natural gas prices in Europe. We're actually really in Energy Island here in Massachusetts. We import much of our LNG, and that LNG that we import is competing for the spot price in Europe. So we're seating home-eating bills this winter, potentially going up by almost $500 over the course of the winter for many of my constituents in the South Coast. It'd be about $200 for many bank constituents closer to Boston. That's going to be very painful for people. I'm acutely aware of that. And it underscores why it's so critical for Massachusetts and the nation to achieve clean energy independence. We need to be in charge of our own destiny. We need to make energy too cheap to meter. And the thing is we know how to do that. We've seen with offshore wind, with geothermal, with solar. We can make investments as we have this Congress to To generate clean renewable energy that can be too cheap to meter and that can provide energy security for residents here in the Bay State. Now, that is our long term aspiration. We know it's not going to happen overnight. We continue to rely on natural gas in the short term and we need to. plus up our low-income heating program and our Northeast home heating oil supplies so that we can help people here in the short term. So I'm very aware that cost of living from making situations is a real struggle right now. There are some things that we're doing to prevent and mitigate that in the short term like capping out of pocket costs for medicines for people on Medicare, but the trade-offs remain. The second big thing besides for cost of living is a lot of anxiety about the increasing extremism of We have seen with women's reproductive rights. We have seen with election denial. It is unnerving to work with these people in Congress. And it's unnerving, I know, from my constituents who are reading headlines that make them feel like they don't recognize their country anymore.
